source.title: Bitter Lessons from Distillation Robustifies Unlearning

record.file_problem: The supplied text is not garbled or cut off. It refers to a figure whose image and numeric values are not included; its panels are described in the text.
record.tranche_reason: The post describes an oracle-matching experiment and fine-tuning relearning attacks that conceptually test whether suppressed knowledge remains recoverable. It does not reproduce the named unlearning methods.
record.gate_note: The post reports qualitative outcomes for fine-tuning on the forget domain, including comparisons among three models. The near-zero KL result is only evidence of matching oracle behavior, not a direct measure of targeted-knowledge accuracy or general ability, so it is not a separate row. Claims about prior unlearning studies are cited background, not rows.
record.test_reason: The post reports the authors' own oracle-matching experiment (small models pretrained from scratch on the Gemma architecture). A student behaviourally matched to a never-trained oracle still relearns the forget capability rapidly under fine-tuning on the forget set. This is a direct result against A and for B. A fresh-initialization student relearns only at the oracle's rate, a result bearing on F. The authors use this to argue that efficient post hoc robust unlearning may be impossible.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The author argues that behavioural suppression differs from capability removal: an oracle-matched model relearns fast because its weights still encode the capability. He concludes that efficient post hoc robust unlearning may be impossible. Robustness requires never learning the capability, or enough damage plus distillation into a fresh or damaged student. He presents distillation, and training-time methods such as gradient routing, as promising routes.
record.recipe_differences: The post describes pretraining reference and oracle models, then matching oracle outputs with either reference weights or random initialization. It does not apply gradient ascent, Who's Harry Potter, RMU, or another named original method.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported relearning outcome depends on initialization and prior exposure: Student (Reference) recovers rapidly, while Student (Random) and Oracle Teacher relearn slowly.
record.problems: The supplied post gives qualitative descriptions but no numerical results, uncertainty estimates, or direct targeted-knowledge and general-ability evaluations. The figure itself is absent. It reports only forget-domain fine-tuning for the relearning attack.
record.rows_left_out: No separate row for the near-zero KL result: it establishes behavioral matching to the oracle but does not directly measure targeted-knowledge recovery or general ability. The text provides no numerical values for the described panels.

untested.parts: No targeted-knowledge accuracy near chance, no general-ability retention, and no named methods (GA, WHP, RMU) are reported numerically in the post.
Relearning-set size is unstated, and unrelated or loosely related relearning data is not tested; only the forget set is used.
No activation ablation or internal analysis. The claim that weights retain structure is inferred only from relearning speed.
Prompting, jailbreaks, other languages and in-context attacks are not tested.
Robustness of fresh-init distillation is tested only against forget-set fine-tuning, not internal edits, quantization or prompting.

missing.what: Numeric relearning curves (panels b-c) for all three models, and the KL-divergence values establishing behavioural match (panel a). The KL result is the baseline that makes the R1 challenge to A meaningful.
missing.locator: 'What our paper actually shows', figure panels a-c; full paper 'Distillation Robustifies Unlearning'

missing.what: The underlying paper's damage-then-distill method (noise plus distillation) and its results against named unlearning methods. The post only alludes to these ('sufficiently damaging the model').
missing.locator: 'What our paper actually shows', final paragraphs; full paper

record.verdict_notes: This is a blog-post summary of the authors' own paper; the figure values are absent, so all rows are qualitative. The record's version ids V1/V2/V3/V6 were invalid and have been remapped to A/B/C/F. C is not linked: the 'weights retain structure' claim rests only on relearning, with no internal analysis. The setting is small models pretrained from scratch, which may limit transfer to large LLM unlearning. Not an original source.

versions.untested_parts: The post does not directly report targeted-knowledge accuracy near chance, preservation of general ability, or tests of gradient ascent, Who's Harry Potter, RMU, and other named methods. It does report relearning after oracle-matched behavior.
The relearning data amount and whether it is a small set, unrelated examples, loosely related examples, or a subset of forgotten facts are not stated; the reported attack uses the forget domain.
No activation-direction ablation is performed. The post's evidence for retained structure is the fast relearning of the oracle-matched reference student.
Prompt rephrasing, jailbreaks, other languages, and in-context information are not tested.
The fresh-initialization distillation approach is evaluated only against fine-tuning on the forget domain, not the other attacks listed in the claim.

relation.reason: The post reports and interprets its own relearning experiment on the claim.

tranche.reason: The post argues from its own oracle-matching result that behavioural matching is not robust unlearning, so versions A and F need restating. It is borderline T2, since it is a different method on the same question. T5 is defensible.

source_check.notes: This is a LessWrong post by an author of 2506.06278, restating that paper's oracle-matching figure. It is not independent evidence, and its results are qualitative with no numbers, sizes or uncertainty. R1's 'observed' state refers to the recovery effect, so for A it means A's robustness fails.

statements.correction: This post (LessWrong, Bruce W. Lee, an author of 2506.06278): Gemma-architecture models pretrained from scratch. Student (Reference) matched to a never-trained oracle (KL near zero) recovers the forget capability rapidly under forget-set fine-tuning. Oracle Teacher and Student (Random) relearn slowly. No numbers, model sizes, step counts or uncertainty.
statements.problem: The statement cites this post's R1 but never names or describes the post. The nearby sentence (GradDiff/MaxEnt/RMU, 0.1B/0.3B, 500 steps, worst-case learning rate) is tagged 2506.06278, and the post reports none of it. The 'why' line leaves the post out.

statements.correction: This post: a randomly initialized student distilled to near-zero KL from the oracle relearns slowly under forget-set fine-tuning, at roughly the oracle's rate. It gives no numbers. The post says sufficient damage is necessary, not sufficient, and that distillation and relearning checks are still needed.
statements.problem: The post is cited under UNDO but gives no 0.1B/0.3B sizes, no synthetic language or arithmetic tasks and no INT4 truth ratio 0.017. Its R3 is Student (Random) distilled from a never-trained oracle, not UNDO (no unlearning or noise step). The 'why' (NeurIPS, uncertainty) describes the paper, not the post.
